blocks.content: SQL SELECT covered choosing which columns you want back. SQL WHERE covers the next genuinely essential piece, filtering rows down to only the ones you actually want, rather than every single row in the table. Without a WHERE clause, a query has no way to narrow its results at all.

This topic covers how WHERE actually works, the comparison operators available, how AND and OR combine multiple conditions, and a genuinely common trap around comparing against NULL that catches even experienced engineers occasionally.
/engineering/library/dbms/images/1785438200062-447041186.png
1. Without WHERE Versus With WHERE
A SELECT with no WHERE clause returns every single row in the table, unconditionally, which is rarely what you actually want once a table has more than a handful of rows.
A SELECT with a genuine WHERE clause returns only the rows that actually match your specified condition, narrowing the result down to exactly what you actually need for a given purpose.
/engineering/library/dbms/images/1785438200063-934837710.png
2. Common Comparison Operators

A few genuinely essential operators show up constantly in WHERE clauses. Equals, greater than, and less than, for direct value comparisons. AND and OR, to combine multiple conditions together into one real, more specific filter.

IN, to match a column against a list of acceptable values in one clean expression, rather than a long chain of OR conditions. And LIKE, to match a text pattern, genuinely useful for searching within text fields rather than requiring an exact match.
/engineering/library/dbms/images/1785438200063-107392254.png

3. A Worked Example
A concrete query shows WHERE applied to a real table. An employees table has a salary column, and a specific query needs only the employees earning above a certain threshold.
SELECT name FROM employees WHERE salary > 80000;
blocks.code: SELECT name FROM employees WHERE salary > 80000;

codes.sql: SELECT name FROM employees WHERE salary > 80000;

blocks.content: This query returns only the names of employees earning above eighty thousand, filtering out every row where that condition is not actually true, without you having to manually sift through the full, unfiltered result yourself.
/engineering/library/dbms/images/1785438200064-509867604.png
4. AND and OR Logic

AND requires every listed condition to genuinely be true for a row to match, department equals Engineering AND salary greater than 90000 only returns engineering employees who also clear that specific salary bar, both conditions must hold together.

OR requires at least one listed condition to be true, department equals Sales OR department equals Marketing returns rows from either department, since only one of the two conditions actually needs to hold for a given row.
/engineering/library/dbms/images/1785438200064-125025240.png

LIKE deserves a closer look, since its pattern syntax is genuinely specific. A percent sign matches any sequence of characters, including none at all, while an underscore matches exactly one single character. A condition like name LIKE the letter A followed by a percent sign matches any name starting with A, regardless of how many characters follow it.
/engineering/library/dbms/images/1785438200275-850220618.png

blocks.title: Common mistake
blocks.content: Mixing AND and OR in one WHERE clause without parentheses to make the actual grouping explicit. SQL applies a real, specific precedence between AND and OR, and relying on that default precedence without parentheses can genuinely produce a different result than you actually intended.
5. The NULL Comparison Trap

Using the equals sign to compare a column against NULL never actually returns true, even when comparing a NULL value against another NULL value, since NULL genuinely represents an unknown value, and SQL treats any comparison against an unknown value as itself unknown, not true.

Using IS NULL specifically is the correct, genuinely working way to check whether a column value is NULL, since it is a dedicated check built for exactly this case, rather than relying on a standard equality comparison that was never designed to handle it correctly.
/engineering/library/dbms/images/1785438200276-461045332.png

blocks.title: Worth remembering
blocks.content: This NULL comparison trap catches even experienced engineers occasionally, since it genuinely contradicts how equality intuitively should work. Remembering to use IS NULL, not equals NULL, is worth committing to memory specifically.
6. Genuinely Common Mistakes

A few real patterns undermine WHERE usage. Using the equals sign to check for NULL, which never actually matches, silently returning fewer rows than genuinely intended. Mixing AND and OR without parentheses, changing the real, actual meaning of the filter without any obvious error being raised.
And forgetting that WHERE runs before column aliases defined in the SELECT clause are genuinely usable, a detail tied to SQL execution order, covered as its own dedicated topic later in this module.
